gens.text:
The channel narrows here between two continents, which the charts render as a pale trench of soundings, and because the seafloor rises without warning from the abyssal plain, the water changes colour above it and the swell steepens into short, quarrelsome ridges, and the island lifts out of that shoaling brightness — a slab of limestone tilted like a table pushed against a wall, its long flank offered to Africa — seeming to hold the whole strait open with one low arm, and the coast that runs west from the harbour breaks into coves so abrupt that a boat must be turned by hand to enter them, since the rock leans out overhead before the sand appears, willing to shelter whatever comes and to hide it afterwards.

Beyond the last cove the shelf drops away into a blue that admits no bottom, that swallows the shadow of any hull crossing it, that draws the eye south toward a horizon too even to be trusted, and the mind goes with it: because the coast of Libya lies four hours beyond sight, because the freighters keep their lanes far to the east, because the small boats come up out of that emptiness at dawn with nothing behind them but the water they have already used.

The island has no rivers, only the memory of them: the wadis that seam its interior, the dry beds walled with prickly pear, where a winter rain runs for one afternoon and is gone before evening.

Salt lies on everything that grows above the cliff line, on the dwarf junipers and the burnt-back caper, and the wind does the rest, scouring the plateau until it holds nothing taller than a man's knee.

The harbour cuts into the southern shore like a thumbprint pressed into soft clay, a basin the fishing fleet has used for centuries and the port authority now numbers in registers, wide enough to swallow a patrol cutter when the sirocco turns the outer roads to chalk, and its mouth is a gate — a gap of two hundred metres that anyone arriving must pass through.

Above the quay stands the low grey building that the coast guard uses to log arrivals, whose radar mast turns all night without hurry, and the antennas of the finance police crown the ridge behind it, where the frontier is not a line drawn on land but a field of listening, which thickens over the water offshore and thins toward the interior, dense enough to register a wooden hull at thirty kilometres and to distinguish a drifting engine from a running one, so that the sea itself becomes an instrument, read in Rome and read again in Warsaw.

The agency's aircraft come over twice daily to draw their long ellipses above the shipping lane, and the shadow of each one crosses the cliffs like a second, faster bird.

Everything here has learned to wait: the cutters at their moorings, the buses idle at the pier, the doctors with their gloves already on, and the interpreters who stand a little apart, and the island itself waits, since waiting is the work the map has assigned it.

The reception centre sits inland in a valley out of view of the town: its fences take the light like water, and no road approaches it directly, so that a visitor must climb the ridge and descend again, and even then sees only the roofs, and hears only the generators.

The geography obliges this discretion in a hundred small ways: the plateau folds where it should be flat, and the tracks bend around old cisterns whose stonework predates every flag that has claimed the place and outlasts each of them in turn; but the arithmetic is plain enough — a rock of twenty square kilometres, which lies nearer to Tunisia than to Sicily, which has been made the doorstep of a continent that begins two hundred kilometres north of it, because the doorstep must be somewhere, and because a border, to be enforced, requires a floor to stand on.

Even so, the fishermen still go out at three in the morning, as their fathers did before the registers.

The lighthouse on the western point turns through the dark with the patience of something that has no opinion, and while its beam sweeps the open water it also sweeps the cliffs, and long before the sky greys it has passed a hundred times over the cemetery of hulls below the customs yard, where the timbers of the boats are stacked by year, and the last of the beam falls on the strait itself, which gives nothing back; the light moves on; the sea keeps its own accounts.

The channel that divides Sicily from the African shelf narrows here into a corridor of open water, and because the seabed lifts abruptly beneath it, the currents crowd upward and the swell steepens without warning, and the island itself sits at the corridor's throat, a low tilted slab of limestone that seems, when seen from the deck of an approaching hull, to have been broken off from a coastline that no longer exists and set adrift southward, so that whatever crosses this stretch must pass within sight of it, whether the crossing is made to be counted or to escape counting, since the water offers no other landmark for two hundred kilometers, nothing to fix a position by except the loom of its harbor lights and the pale scar of its runway.

It is an island of eighteen or so square kilometers, whose highest ground barely reaches a hundred and thirty meters, whose northern cliffs fall sheer into a sea that has undercut them for millennia, whose southern flank slopes gently enough to admit a single cove of white shelving sand; and the geology explains the rest — because the cliffs forbid landing, because the cove is shallow and eastward, because the port lies where the limestone folds inward and holds still water.

Along that fold the quays run in a shallow arc, doubled by concrete: on the inner side the fishing boats lie gunwale to gunwale, while on the outer side the grey patrol hulls keep their berths clear.

Beyond the last bollard stands a compound of prefabricated blocks, whose roofs are ribbed aluminum bleached almost white; and behind it rises a fence of galvanized mesh that follows the contour of the valley floor.

The compound occupies a dry watercourse called the Imbriacola, which drains nothing now and has drained nothing since the last of the springs failed, and it was built to hold four hundred people until the ferries came; but its registers record other figures, figures too large to be spoken of as capacity.

Along the ridge above it runs the coastal track, worn to bedrock in places by the tires of the vehicles that climb it hourly, a track that no map marks as military, and from the head of that track the whole basin is legible: the roofs below, the harbor mouth beyond, and the horizon southward, where the water changes color over the shelf edge and the radar mast turns on its concrete plinth, sweeping a circle it has swept without interruption for twenty years, unless the wind rises past a certain force and the dish is locked down.

Farther east the airfield takes the width of the island, a strip long enough to land transport aircraft, and its perimeter lights burn all night above the prickly pear.

The apparatus is layered like the rock itself: seaward first, the cutters and the tenders; then the helicopters; then the cameras on their poles, and the thermal lenses that see the sea as a field of temperatures; and last the offices, where the fingerprints are taken and the papers begin.

Each layer has its own vocabulary and its own hours; the cutters work the darkness, and the offices work the morning, so that a body pulled from the water at four is a name by nine, or a number, or a hyphenated entry in a column, or nothing at all.

The island answers all of it with the same indifference it offers to the sirocco: the dust settles on the mesh, and the salt eats the galvanizing from the wire that the crews replace each spring, though the replacement never quite holds; and there is a small cemetery on the western slope, whose stones bear dates and no names, which the wind has smoothed until the numerals themselves grow shallow, because nothing here resists the abrasion of air and salt for long, not stone, not paint, not memory, unless someone tends it deliberately.

Below the cemetery lies the boat graveyard, where the hulls are stacked three deep in painted wood.

They are the plainest documents on the island, these hulls that no archive has accessioned, and while some are seven meters and some are twenty, and while the paint on the older ones has faded to the color of the rock they lie against, the shapes are unmistakable to anyone who has watched them come in, and they hold rainwater in their bilges after a storm, water that the sun takes back within a day; the island keeps almost nothing, and gives up almost nothing either.

The channel that divides Africa from Europe narrows here into a shallow trough of water, and where the seabed lifts toward the last shelf of limestone before the open deep, it lets go of its indigo and turns the colour of glass held to a lamp, and the horizon loses its ruled edge, and the whole southern quarter of the map thins into a scattering of small hard islands that seem to have been shaken loose from the continent behind them, one of them lying flatter and drier than the rest, so pale in the noon light that a pilot might mistake it for a sandbar until the radar returns insist otherwise, until the runway shows as a grey stripe laid across it, and then the eye consents to read it as land, and the charts agree.

The island is a wedge of pitted rock, whose northern flank falls in unbroken cliffs to water eighty metres deep, whose southern slope shelves gently into coves of white marl, whose whole surface has been scoured by wind too steady to permit a tree; and the wind is the first fact of the place, since nothing stands upright here that has not been braced, since the cactus grows sideways, since even the harbour lights lean.

Between the cliffs and the coves the settlement gathers itself along a single ridge of packed houses, and it does not spread, though the airfield behind it has doubled twice in thirty years and now takes more traffic than the fishery ever did.

The port is a hooked basin of dark water, whose mouth swings east against the prevailing weather, and it holds two kinds of vessel, whose hulls announce their business before their flags do.

On the seaward mole stand the grey cutters of the coastguard, whose decks are stacked with orange life-rings and folded stretchers, ready to slip their lines when the radio room calls a position; and behind them lie the impounded boats, whose blue paint has begun to lift and curl.

Above the basin, on a shoulder of rock that offers a clear sightline to the channel, sits the low white building that the mainland calls a centre, and it is fenced twice over, with a perimeter of steel mesh that follows the contour of the hill, and a second, inner line of bollards and cameras that watch the gate, and record the yard, and require of every arrival a number, so that the register may close each evening, and the tally may be signalled north.

The road from the quay to that gate is two kilometres of white dust, easy to walk in the dark, and buses take it four or five times a week.

Everything on the island has been arranged to face the water: the watchtower, the radar mast, the mooring rings; the fishermen read the swell for their nets, and the officers read it for their sailings; and the two readings converge in September, when the sea flattens.

Nothing here is hidden, and nothing is explained: the cliffs declare their strata plainly, and the boats are counted at dawn, while a helicopter goes out at first light and comes back at nine, and goes out again at dusk, and the log fills.

To the south there is nothing charted for a hundred and thirteen kilometres but the shipping lanes and the drifting rafts, and to the north the nearest port of the mainland lies further than the coast the boats set out from; so that the island sits between two shores, each of which claims it in a different language, which the customs stamp settles by printing a European word, though the water carries an African wind, and has always carried it.

There is one cemetery on the ridge, in which a row of unmarked stones is kept level with a rake.

The visitor who climbs to the lighthouse at evening sees the whole arrangement at once, laid out as a diagram: the harbour with its two fleets, and beyond the harbour the white fence tracing its contour, while the runway lights come on in sequence and the patrol boat clears the mole; and the channel opens south into a haze that no lamp reaches, in which the horizon has already gone; and the wind does not drop.

The channel that divides Africa from Europe narrows here into a corridor of blue that the charts colour with false confidence, and where the seabed climbs toward the Pelagie shelf it loses its abyssal darkness and takes on the pale, grazed green of shallows, and it lifts at last a small limestone raft, hardly eight miles long, which the wind has scoured to the bone and which seems, from the deck of any approaching hull, to gather the whole traffic of the strait into one low rim of rock, so that a vessel steering north must pass within sight of it before the coast of Sicily rises, as though the island had been set there deliberately to inspect what crosses, and to be crossed in turn.

Lampedusa, which is nearer to Tunisia than to the country that governs it, which faces south with its cliffs and north with its single harbour, which has learned to receive what the current delivers and to count it, lies at the hinge of two arithmetics; the sea brings numbers ashore, the state converts them into files, the island holds the difference between the two.

The southern shore is a wall of white rock scalloped by caves, and the caves keep their cold all summer, while above them the garrigue runs flat and grey to the runway fence.

The harbour is a cleft in that wall, a narrow water the colour of bottle glass, and along its quay the patrol boats lie in a grey row, whose hulls carry the tricolour band and the pale blue lettering of the Guardia Costiera.

Beyond the mole a second fleet swings at its moorings, the fishing boats that go out for lampuga and return before noon, too small to be mistaken for anything else when the radar sweeps at night; and behind them, half-hauled onto the concrete, sit the wooden carcasses that no one has yet decided to burn.

The apparatus that has settled on this rock, in order to see everything that approaches it, is topography now as much as the limestone is: the mast on the high ground, the radar dome that turns without sound above Cala Croce, and the aerostat tethered over the airstrip, whose cable hums in the maestrale, whose eye reads the water for sixty miles, so that the boats are known before they are seen, and so that a crossing is a curve on a screen in Warsaw or in Pratica di Mare, a line drawn to converge with another line, long before any hand reaches over a gunwale and takes hold of another hand.

The hotspot lies inland in the Imbriacola valley, a low compound of prefabricated blocks set to hold three hundred, and its fence follows the contour of the ground like a dry-stone wall.

The road that climbs to it from the port is short enough to walk, but no one walks it; the buses go up in convoy, and the blue lights turn on the rock faces, and the dust settles again as soon as the last vehicle has passed.

Everything on the island is arranged around this passage: the pier where the disembarkations are counted, the tent where the medics work, and the gate where the tally is made final, because a name written down at the gate becomes a fingerprint, and the fingerprint becomes a jurisdiction, and the jurisdiction becomes the reason a person may not board the ferry to Porto Empedocle.

Above all this the plateau lies bare and windswept: there is little soil, there are no rivers, and there is one road that runs the length of the island, past the cemetery and the desalination plant, whose pumps sound faintly at night; and there is the airfield, which takes the charter flights that leave after dark, which carry the transferred to Sicily or to Calabria, so that the compound may be emptied before the next weather window opens, ready to fill again, as it always fills within the week.

From the highest ground the sea shows on three sides at once, an unbroken ring that offers the eye no landmark whatever.

At dawn the island is at its plainest, a slab of pale stone that the light strikes flatly, and when the haze lifts off the water the horizon hardens and the strait shows its true width, so wide that nothing can be distinguished on it except the wake of the cutter that goes out each morning to the twelve-mile line; and the gulls follow it as far as the buoy, which marks nothing but a change of law; then the island returns to its own silence, the fences ticking in the heat, the radar turning, the sea arriving.

The channel that divides Africa from Europe narrows here into a shallow trench of pale water, and where the seabed lifts toward the shelf it throws up a single low table of limestone, scoured of trees, ringed with white cliffs on its northern flank and sloping southward into coves the colour of bottle glass, so that the island seems less a fragment of either continent than a raft anchored midway, a stone that the currents have polished from both sides, which the fishermen once knew simply as the last land, and which now compels every passing hull to declare itself, since no vessel may cross this parallel unregistered, so that even a skiff of eight metres, drifting without an engine, must be counted before the light fails, and its people photographed and named.

The coast that faces south is a run of terraces broken by sudden inlets, whose sand is coarse and grey with pumice, whose thorn scrub holds the salt like a sponge, and which the summer wind strips down to bare rock, to leave the marl exposed and chalky underfoot; and the whole shelf tilts as the water tilts, as the wind tilts the dry grasses inland, as the light tilts through the long afternoons of the crossing season.

To the east the ground rises in a series of shallow steps toward the airfield, and the runway lies flat along the spine of the island, though from the harbour road nothing of it shows but a windsock and a fence.

The harbour itself is a hooked basin, whose entrance the moles nearly close, and the trawlers lie three deep against the quay, where the grey cutters of the coastal service take the outermost berth.

Beyond the last warehouse a track climbs between prickly pear and low walls, which the goats have loosened and the rains have opened, seeming to end at the ridge, until it turns and drops again; and there, in the hollow, stand the long white sheds of the reception centre, whose gates are worked from a booth to admit the buses.

The apparatus that governs this hollow is not a building but a system, arranged to convert arrival into paper, which the island wears as it wears its cisterns and its aerials; and it has offices along the port road, whose windows are shuttered against the glare, and patrol boats moored in the second basin, which slip out before dawn and return heavy with the morning, and which the radar tower above the lighthouse tracks continually, to hold the whole southern approach in a single revolving beam, while the aircraft of the frontier agency draw their slow ellipses offshore and the satellites pass unheard.

The tower is set to command the horizon, and its antennae turn day and night above the scrub, indifferent to the weather.

The lighthouse, older, still keeps its arc across the same water; the two are neighbours; the one warns and the other watches, and each has learned the other's rhythm, so that their sweeps cross without collision.

The plateau carries little else: a cemetery of numbered markers, a chapel, and a reservoir sunk into rock, while the roads run out into dust at the perimeter fences, where the wire is doubled, where the signage repeats itself in four languages, and where the wind fills the mesh with plastic.

From the cliff path the whole arrangement lies open at once: the basin with its cutters, the sheds with their courtyards, which the sun bleaches by noon and the floodlights hold all night; and the sea beyond, which carries the traffic that the tower counts, which the boats intercept and the registers absorb, until each crossing has been folded into a file, to be forwarded northward through offices that have never seen this rock, while the water closes and the horizon gives up nothing.

The island is small enough to be walked in a morning by anyone who cares to try.

Yet its function is enormous, and the traveller who climbs to the ridge at evening feels the disproportion sharply, because the land beneath him is barely six kilometres of stone, and because the sea around it holds a jurisdiction that reaches to the Libyan shore, whose margins no map here draws; and the light goes out of the water gradually, which the fences catch last of all, holding it in bright lines; then the generators start, and the sheds come up white against the dark.

The channel that divides Sicily from the African shelf narrows here into a shallow trough, and where the seabed lifts into a limestone shoulder it throws up a single pale island, scarcely eight miles long, whose cliffs face south toward a coast that lies nearer to it than its own province does; and the island stands in that water like a stone set on the lip of a threshold, so exact in its position that the maps drawn in northern offices seem to have placed it there deliberately, as if some cartographer had wished to fix a marker at the seam of two continents, so that whoever crossed the water would have to pass beneath its lamps, and would learn, before touching any harbour, that arrival is a thing administered and not merely reached.

The island's spine, which tilts from the low northern flats toward the sheer southern wall, which holds no river and almost no soil, which offers the wind nothing to break its run, seems to have been shaped for surveillance; the ground is bare, the sightlines are long, the horizon at noon is a single unbroken wire of light.

From the height above the port the whole southern quadrant opens at once, and the eye takes it in without effort: the bay, the two coves, the white gravel of the shore, the water shading from glass to indigo where the shelf drops away.

Below the ridge lies the harbour basin, which cuts a deep notch into the rock; along its quays the grey hulls of the patrol vessels ride at their moorings, their numbers stencilled in black on plating that the salt has already begun to pit.

Beyond the mole the open channel begins, which carries the freight of the whole crossing and takes back very little of it, seeming to widen as the afternoon light flattens; and on its far edge, invisible, lies the departure coast whose beaches send out the inflatables at night.

The road that climbs from the quay, tending always to bear inland, that passes the fuel depot and the shuttered cannery, runs at last to the compound above the valley, whose fences carry a double crown of wire, whose gates are watched from a raised booth by men in blue coveralls who log each vehicle and radio the numbers up the hill, and who have learned to read the sea's temper as farmers read a sky, since a flat night in April means arrivals before dawn, and the buses will be waiting with their engines running.

The compound was built to hold four hundred, and on many mornings it holds three times that number in a yard of packed white dust.

The apparatus that grew to meet the crossing is itself a kind of terrain: there are the radar masts on the eastern point, and the aerostat that rises above them in fair weather, and the drone strip inland, whose grey machines lift at dusk when the thermals slacken.

Everything here is registered: the boats are counted, the bodies are counted, and the counting proceeds so steadily that the ledgers acquire the authority of rock, and the numbers outlast the faces, and the season is remembered by its totals.

Consider that shore on any clear morning in the migration months, and the pattern declares itself: the cutters go out at first light, and the helicopter tracks a widening spiral above the shipping lane, whose crews report by encrypted link and mark each contact on a screen; consider also the smaller apparatus, the interpreters who wait at the pier in reflective vests, whose lists carry names transliterated four different ways, while a doctor moves down the line with a thermometer, checking for fever before the sorting begins, before anyone is asked where he sailed from.

Yet the island itself keeps a stubborn indifference that no fence has managed to reorganize.

The prickly pear holds the terraces, which no one has farmed in fifty years; and when the sirocco comes up out of the south the dust reddens on the windowsills and the ferry cancels, so that for two days nothing crosses at all except the wind, which finds the wire and sings in it; and the fishermen mend their nets in the lee of the boathouses, where the radios murmur their coordinates all afternoon; the sea meanwhile lies down, empty, blue, and perfectly legible.

The channel that separates the African shelf from the last crumb of Europe narrows here into a corridor of water no wider than a night's drifting, and because the current runs east with the season and the wind comes down off the Gulf of Gabès in long dry pushes, the sea arranges itself into lanes as legible as roads, lanes that the fishermen have read for four hundred years, lanes that now oblige a second kind of reading, since a hull that leaves the Libyan sandbar at dusk, a hull whose freeboard is measured in fingers rather than feet, will cross a boundary invisible to everyone aboard, and when the plotters ashore begin to score its position, the vessel ceases to be a boat in order that it may become, before anyone has seen a face, a contact, an object to be resolved, a number that thickens on a screen.

The island itself is a low limestone wedge, whose northern coast rises into cliffs the colour of old bone, whose southern shore slides down to coves of pale grit, whose whole surface seems to want to lie flatter than it does; and it sits nearer to Africa than to Sicily, so that the maps drawn in Brussels place it always at their bottom edge, though the maps drawn in the harbour place it at the centre, while the maps drawn nowhere at all place it simply at the end.

Nothing on it is high enough to be called a hill; there is only the slow tilt of the plateau, the scrub, the dry-stone walls, until the land stops without warning at the rim.

The harbour lies in a notch on the southeast flank, a notch that the swell rarely enters; two moles enclose it, and along the inner mole are berthed the grey hulls whose numbers are painted small.

Everything here is written in acronyms that the eye learns before the mouth does: the letters stencilled on the patrol boats, the letters on the shipping containers behind the fence, and above them the mast that keeps turning to look at an emptiness, as if the emptiness could be persuaded to declare itself; the antennas do the same, antennas whose only appetite is to hear.

Above the town, on the ridge road, stands a compound that the guidebooks decline to name, a compound of prefabricated modules and a running track of dust, and it is called a centre of first reception and assistance, a phrase that has outlasted several ministries, a phrase that hides a gate, that hides a register, and that hides the hour of the morning when the buses come down to the quay in order to be filled and emptied again, before the shops have opened, though the bakers are awake and the light has already come off the water.

The mole has a rhythm of its own, easy to learn and impossible to forget, and it belongs to arrival rather than to departure.

There is a way of standing that the officers acquire within a month: the weight back, the clipboard low; the gloves come out, and the numbers go on; the wrists are counted and the children are counted twice, because the count is what survives.

Around this the ordinary island continues: the prickly pear holds the terraces, and the goats work the scrub as they have always worked it, while the ferry comes up from Porto Empedocle on its schedule, the tourists come down the gangway in their sandals, the divers go out to the wreck at the Rabbit Beach shallows.

Two economies share one quay: the fish are landed at dawn, and the ice is broken over them, ice that comes from a plant behind the fuel tanks and that whitens the concrete for an hour; and above the same concrete the radar sweeps, sweeps for a hull that no chart records, that no owner claims, so that when the sighting is finally made, the boats go out to meet it, though nobody ashore stops what he is doing.

There is a small cemetery at the edge of town, where some of the graves carry no name.

Beyond it the plateau runs out to the western cliffs, which fall two hundred feet into water of a blue that admits no bottom, and because the wind has scoured the soil to a thin brown skin and nothing grows tall, so that the eye finds no interruption between the airstrip and the horizon that the radar keeps combing, a person standing there can see the whole apparatus at once, an apparatus that has taken the shape of the island as water takes the shape of a jar; and the island, for its part, has taken the shape of the apparatus.

The channel that divides Sicily from the African shelf narrows here into a corridor of open water, whose colour changes with the depth of the shelf beneath it, and where the seabed climbs toward the last outcrop of Europe the swell begins to shorten and the light on the surface hardens, so that a traveller coming north sees the island only as a low grey interruption, which lies flatter than any coast has a right to lie, seeming to float rather than to rest, and the rock that carries it, tilted long ago toward Africa and worn smooth on its southern face, holds its cliffs high on the northern side, as if to shelter the one harbour that opens there, so narrow that a vessel must slow to enter, and the engines fall silent.

Lampedusa is a slab of pale limestone twenty kilometres square, which grows nothing taller than a caper bush, which keeps no river and no spring, which has learned to catch its water from the roofs and hold it in cisterns; the wind here is the true landlord, since it comes from the southeast in August loaded with red dust, since it comes from the northwest in winter and strips the terraces bare, since it never entirely stops.

From the airstrip a single road runs the length of the plateau; it passes the cemetery, the fuel depot, the shuttered greenhouses, before it drops into the valley behind the town where the reception centre stands.

The centre is a compound of prefabricated blocks, which were built for four hundred and have held two thousand; behind them rises a fence of galvanised mesh, which the salt air has already begun to flower with rust.

Above the gate a camera turns on its mounting, which sweeps the yard in a slow arc and returns; the men beneath it have stopped looking up, unless a new shift arrives at the hour; and there is a second lens on the water tower, which is angled to watch the road rather than the sea.

The police apparatus on this island has the permanence of geology: an office of the Questura that keeps its lights on until dawn, a detachment of the Guardia di Finanza whose grey patrol boats moor at the inner quay, and beyond them the European agency maintains its own presence, which is neither garrison nor embassy, which arrives in rotations of six weeks, brings its own interpreters and its own laptops, and files its counts to Warsaw each morning, in order to appear in a table of figures before the sun has cleared the eastern headland and the first bus has climbed the hill.

The rhythm of the place is set by these arrivals, to be read in the movement of vehicles at three in the morning, and nothing else on the island keeps such punctual hours.

The quay itself is short, stone-built, cheaply repaired; the bollards are new, the paving is not; and the fishing fleet has been pushed to the far mole, where the water is shallower than the cutters draw.

Beyond the mole the coast turns west into a country of coves; the limestone gives way in staircases, and the sea has hollowed the base of every headland, so that caves run back into the rock, some open to the sky, some closed and full of echo.

Off the southwest corner lies the small islet the maps call Rabbit Island; the sand there is white and fine, the water is clear to eight metres, and the loggerhead turtles come ashore in July, which the wardens fence off and guard through the nesting weeks; and half a mile out, on the same clean floor, lie the timbers of boats that were not fenced or guarded, that settled where they filled, when there was nothing left to do but wait for a hull to be raised or written off, after the divers had finished their work.

The tourists swim above these places in August, which is a thing the island has stopped remarking on.

What remains is the shape of the rock itself, which the sea has been trimming for six million years, and though the fences change with the ministries and the cameras are replaced with better cameras every second summer, while the paint on the patrol boats is renewed in a shade that the light bleaches within a season, the cliffs keep their line and the cisterns keep their water, which no directive has yet reorganised; the island is simply the last high ground before the water opens.

The channel that divides Sicily from the African shelf narrows here into a corridor of shallow water, and because the seabed rises without warning toward the south, the swell steepens and the current bends eastward, running past a limestone table that lifts barely a hundred metres above the surface and appears, from the deck of any approaching hull, to be a pale interruption in a horizon that otherwise offers nothing, so that a pilot, having no landmark to steer by until the cliffs whiten in the late morning, must trust the compass and hold his line, waiting for the light on the cape to declare itself before he can turn in toward the harbour, and even then the entrance stays hidden until the last mile.

The island itself is a slab of tilted rock, whose northern face drops sheer into water the colour of ink, whose southern slope descends in terraces of dust and prickly pear, whose single deep inlet has for centuries permitted small craft to lie safe from the northwesterlies; and the town crowds the head of that inlet, though the cemetery stands apart on the rise, though the airstrip takes the whole flat waist of the island, though the fuel tanks sit above the quay like a second, duller village.

Beyond the last houses the ground goes bare, and it stays bare for two kilometres, until a fence of galvanised mesh, four metres high and topped with a rolled coil, closes the mouth of a dry valley where the reception centre lies.

The road that serves it is asphalt for the first stretch and gravel afterwards, and it ends at a gate whose two lamps burn all night against the pale flank of the hill.

Below the gate a hangar of ribbed steel holds the arrival hall, which was built for two hundred and has held two thousand, and which is easier to enter than to leave, since the exit is a corridor of numbered doors; and above it, on the ridge, stands the mast whose dishes turn slowly to track the patrol aircraft offshore.

The apparatus that governs this water is best described as a relief map, a thing of contour and gradient rather than of intention, whose lowest layer is the harbour post of the Guardia Costiera, whose upper layers thin out toward the mainland: the finance police keep three cutters at the mole, and the agency in Warsaw keeps a drone circuit, a long oval traced above the Strait of Sicily, which the operators fly from a screen in Pratica di Mare, so that the island is watched from four hundred kilometres away and the watchers never smell the diesel.

The registers accumulate in a room behind the hall, ledgers of fingerprints and hand-drawn deck plans, and no one has ever counted them all.

The vocabulary follows the terrain: hotspot for the hangar, transfer for the ferry at dawn, and the sea itself is divided, on the charts, into zones of responsibility that end where the Libyan claim begins.

Everything here has two names, the fishermen's and the ministry's, and the second name travels farther, because it can be typed into a form, filed in Rome, and read in Brussels by an official who will never see the cliffs.

From the cemetery wall you can take in the whole arrangement at once: the inlet, the mole, the fence, and beyond them the flat blue plate of the channel, on which the wakes of the cutters are drawn and erased, and the eye, which wants a shape to settle on, finds only the mast and the tanks, and the long white scar of the runway, which cuts the island in half as cleanly as a border drawn by a ruler across a country nobody surveyed.

There are days when the haze closes the horizon entirely, and then the island seems to be the only solid thing in creation.

The wind that clears it comes from the northwest, and when it has scoured the sky for a day and a night, the coast of Tunisia appears as a grey thread on the rim of the water, close enough that the distance seems an insult rather than a fact; and the boats come on those days, the small blue ones with the outboards lashed to a transom of scrap plank, and the sirens start in the harbour before the hulls are even visible from the cape.

The channel that separates the two continents narrows here into a corridor of water whose colour changes with the depth of the seabed beneath it, and because the currents from the east push steadily against the shelf, the surface wrinkles into long parallel seams and the swell arrives out of order, so that the small island lying nearest the African shore, which the charts print in a type too fine for its importance, seems to float rather than to rest, though anyone who has approached it at first light and has watched the cliffs assemble themselves out of the haze will understand that, in order to be seen at all, it must be found before the sun climbs high enough to flatten the rock into a single glare and dissolve the outline entirely.

It is a low limestone table, tilted toward the south, which the wind has scoured of everything but thyme and salt-burnt scrub, which holds no river and almost no soil, which has learned to keep its water in cisterns rather than to spend it on green, and everything on it is measured by that scarcity: the houses crouch where the rock permits, the harbour bites into the one flank the weather spares, the airstrip runs where nothing else would grow.

To the north the sea opens without interruption toward the Sicilian channel, and the horizon there is never entirely empty, since something is always standing off at the edge of it, grey-hulled and patient.

The coast on the eastern side is a series of coves cut into pale stone, each of which ends in a fan of shingle; the fishermen have names for all of them, and the manifests that reach the prefecture have numbers, which is not the same knowledge.

Above the largest cove sits the mole, a curve of poured concrete that the last century laid down and the present one has reinforced, wide enough to take a cutter alongside when the sirocco has driven every smaller craft into shelter; from the mole a road climbs the escarpment, which the patrol vehicles use to reach the plateau without passing through the town.

The plateau itself is a treeless flat of dry stone walls, which the goats have worn into terraces too shallow to farm, whose only tall structures are the aerials, and among the aerials stands a radar mast whose dish turns without hurry, and beyond it a fenced enclosure of prefabricated blocks lies in the hollow, and a service track runs from the gate to the road so that supplies may be brought up quietly, since the vehicles are unmarked and the drivers keep their windows shut against the dust.

The fence is double, aluminium posts driven into drilled rock to hold the mesh upright, and a strip of raked ground lies between the two lines.

Beyond the enclosure the ground continues to rise, then breaks; the southern cliffs drop two hundred feet to the water and take the full weight of the open sea, and the surf sounds there all year, though the town, in its bowl, hears almost none of it.

South of that edge there is nothing charted for a hundred miles: the seabed falls away, and the vessels that cross it leave no track, for the water closes behind a hull as it closes behind a swimmer, and the wind erases what the water has smoothed, and the satellites record only heat.

The apparatus that watches this emptiness is arranged in rings, and the rings do not quite meet: the outermost is airborne, a turboprop describing slow ovals at eight thousand feet, and inside it lie the cutters, whose fuel dictates how far south they may loiter and whose orders dictate how long; then, nearer in, come the shore stations, the optical towers set on the two headlands, the men who read the screens in the room above the harbour office, who are told where to look before they look, so that the sea, in order to be surveyed, must first be divided into squares and numbered, as the island itself was numbered on the charts.

Everything here is thus a matter of lines drawn on water, which the water declines to keep.

And so the island holds its position at the hinge of two seas, which is also the hinge of two jurisdictions, and because the rock has never been able to feed the people who stand on it and because the traffic that arrives has never asked the rock's permission, the place has become an instrument for reading a distance it cannot cross, and every structure on it — the mole, the mast, the fence, the road that avoids the town — is an answer to the same question, which nobody on the plateau has ever formulated aloud; the wind, meanwhile, keeps to the south, and the cisterns fill only in December.
